If a symlink is specified, it will be resolved to its target. pattern A regular expression, to be matched using Python's :py:func:`~re.search`. repl The replacement text count: 0 Maximum number of pattern occurrences to be replaced. If count is a positive integer ``n``, only ``n`` occurrences will be replaced, otherwise all occurrences will be replaced. flags (list or int) A list of flags defined in the ``re`` module documentation from the Python standard library. Each list item should be a string that will correlate to the human-friendly flag name. E.g., ``['IGNORECASE', 'MULTILINE']``. Optionally, ``flags`` may be an int, with a value corresponding to the XOR (``|``) of all the desired flags. Defaults to 8 (which supports 'MULTILINE'). bufsize (int or str) How much of the file to buffer into memory at once. The default value ``1`` processes one line at a time. The special value ``file`` may be specified which will read the entire file into memory before processing. append_if_not_found: False New in version 2014.7.0 If set to ``True``, and pattern is not found, then the content will be appended to the file. prepend_if_not_found: False New in version 2014.7.0 If set to ``True`` and pattern is not found, then the content will be prepended to the file. not_found_content New in version 2014.7.0 Content to use for append/prepend if not found. If None (default), uses ``repl``. Useful when ``repl`` uses references to group in pattern. backup: .bak The file extension to use for a backup of the file before editing. Set to ``False`` to skip making a backup. dry_run: False If set to ``True``, no changes will be made to the file, the function will just return the changes that would have been made (or a ``True``/``False`` value if ``show_changes`` is set to ``False``). search_only: False If set to true, this no changes will be performed on the file, and this function will simply return ``True`` if the pattern was matched, and ``False`` if not. show_changes: True If ``True``, return a diff of changes made. Otherwise, return ``True`` if changes were made, and ``False`` if not. Note: Using this option will store two copies of the file in memory (the original version and the edited version) in order to generate the diff. This may not normally be a concern, but could impact performance if used with large files. ignore_if_missing: False New in version 2015.8.0 If set to ``True``, this function will simply return ``False`` if the file doesn't exist. Otherwise, an error will be thrown. preserve_inode: True New in version 2015.8.0 Preserve the inode of the file, so that any hard links continue to share the inode with the original filename. This works by *copying* the file, reading from the copy, and writing to the file at the original inode. If ``False``, the file will be *moved* rather than copied, and a new file will be written to a new inode, but using the original filename. Hard links will then share an inode with the backup, instead (if using ``backup`` to create a backup copy). backslash_literal: False New in version 2016.11.7 Interpret backslashes as literal backslashes for the repl and not escape characters. Create an image for a specific platform. Please note that this function *MUST* be run as root, as images that are created make files belonging to root. platform Which platform to use to create the image. Currently supported platforms are rpm, deb and pacman. root Local path to create the root of the image filesystem. img_format Which format to create the image in. Future support will exist for ``sparse``. fs_format When using a non-``dir`` ``img_format``, which filesystem to format the image to. By default, ``ext2``. fs_opts When using a non-``dir`` ``img_format``, a dict of opts may be specified. arch Architecture to install packages for, if supported by the underlying bootstrap tool. Currently only used for deb. flavor Which flavor of operating system to install. This correlates to a specific directory on the distribution repositories. For instance, ``wheezy`` on Debian. repo_url Mainly important for Debian-based repos. Base URL for the mirror to install from. (e.x.: http://ftp.debian.org/debian/) static_qemu Local path to the static qemu binary required for this arch. (e.x.: /usr/bin/qemu-amd64-static) pkg_confs The location of the conf files to copy into the image, to point the installer to the right repos and configuration. img_size If img_format is not ``dir``, then the size of the image must be specified. mount_dir If img_format is not ``dir``, then the image must be mounted somewhere. If the ``mount_dir`` is not specified, then it will be created at ``/opt/salt-genesis.<random_uuid>``. This directory will be unmounted and removed when the process is finished. pkg_cache This points to a directory containing a cache of package files to be copied to the image. It does not need to be specified. pkgs A list of packages to be installed on this image. For RedHat, this will include ``yum``, ``centos-release`` and ``iputils`` by default. exclude_pkgs A list of packages to be excluded. If you do not want to install the defaults, you need to include them in this list. epel_url The URL to download the EPEL release package from. New in version 0.17.0 Look up the given grain in a given dictionary for the current OS and return the result Although this may occasionally be useful at the CLI, the primary intent of this function is for use in Jinja to make short work of creating lookup tables for OS-specific data. For example: {% set apache = salt['grains.filter_by']({ 'Debian': {'pkg': 'apache2', 'srv': 'apache2'}, 'RedHat': {'pkg': 'httpd', 'srv': 'httpd'}, }, default='Debian') %} myapache: pkg.installed: - name: {{ apache.pkg }} service.running: - name: {{ apache.srv }} Values in the lookup table may be overridden by values in Pillar. An example Pillar to override values in the example above could be as follows: apache: lookup: pkg: apache_13 srv: apache The call to ``filter_by()`` would be modified as follows to reference those Pillar values: {% set apache = salt['grains.filter_by']({ ... }, merge=salt['pillar.get']('apache:lookup')) %} :param lookup_dict: A dictionary, keyed by a grain, containing a value or values relevant to systems matching that grain. For example, a key could be the grain for an OS and the value could the name of a package on that particular OS. Changed in version 2016.11.0 The dictionary key could be a globbing pattern. The function will return the corresponding ``lookup_dict`` value where grain value matches the pattern. For example: # this will render 'got some salt' if Minion ID begins from 'salt' salt '*' grains.filter_by '{salt*: got some salt, default: salt is not here}' id :param grain: The name of a grain to match with the current system's grains. For example, the value of the "os_family" grain for the current system could be used to pull values from the ``lookup_dict`` dictionary. Changed in version 2016.11.0 The grain value could be a list. The function will return the ``lookup_dict`` value for a first found item in the list matching one of the ``lookup_dict`` keys. :param merge: A dictionary to merge with the results of the grain selection from ``lookup_dict``. This allows Pillar to override the values in the ``lookup_dict``. This could be useful, for example, to override the values for non-standard package names such as when using a different Python version from the default Python version provided by the OS (e.g., ``python26-mysql`` instead of ``python-mysql``). :param default: default lookup_dict's key used if the grain does not exists or if the grain value has no match on lookup_dict. Append a rule to the specified table/chain. This function accepts a rule in a standard iptables command format, starting with the chain. Trying to force users to adapt to a new method of creating rules would be irritating at best, and we already have a parser that can handle it. CLI Example: salt '*' iptables.append filter INPUT \ rule='-m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT' IPv6: salt '*' iptables.append filter INPUT \ rule='-m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT' \ family=ipv6 iptables.build_rule:
Build a well-formatted iptables rule based on kwargs. A `table` and `chain` are not required, unless `full` is True. If `full` is `True`, then `table`, `chain` and `command` are required. `command` may be specified as either a short option ('I') or a long option (`--insert`). This will return the iptables command, exactly as it would be used from the command line. If a position is required (as with `-I` or `-D`), it may be specified as `position`. This will only be useful if `full` is True. If `state` is passed, it will be ignored, use `connstate`. If `connstate` is passed in, it will automatically be changed to `state`. To pass in jump options that doesn't take arguments, pass in an empty string. Note: Whereas iptables will accept ``-p``, ``--proto[c[o[l]]]`` as synonyms of ``--protocol``, if ``--proto`` appears in an iptables command after the appearance of ``-m policy``, it is interpreted as the ``--proto`` option of the policy extension (see the iptables-extensions(8) man page). CLI Examples: salt '*' iptables.build_rule match=state \ connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED jump=ACCEPT salt '*' iptables.build_rule filter INPUT command=I position=3 \ full=True match=state connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED jump=ACCEPT salt '*' iptables.build_rule filter INPUT command=A \ full=True match=state connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED \ source='127.0.0.1' jump=ACCEPT .. Invert Rules salt '*' iptables.build_rule filter INPUT command=A \ full=True match=state connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED \ source='!127.0.0.1' jump=ACCEPT salt '*' iptables.build_rule filter INPUT command=A \ full=True match=state connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED \ destination='not 127.0.0.1' jump=ACCEPT IPv6: salt '*' iptables.build_rule match=state \ connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED jump=ACCEPT \ family=ipv6 salt '*' iptables.build_rule filter INPUT command=I position=3 \ full=True match=state connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED jump=ACCEPT \ family=ipv6 iptables.check:

New in version 3006.0 Evaluate each pair of arguments up to the last one as a (matcher, value) tuple, returning ``value`` if matched. If none match, returns the last argument. The ``ifelse`` function is like a multi-level if-else statement. It was inspired by CFEngine's ``ifelse`` function which in turn was inspired by Oracle's ``DECODE`` function. It must have an odd number of arguments (from 1 to N). The last argument is the default value, like the ``else`` clause in standard programming languages. Every pair of arguments before the last one are evaluated as a pair. If the first one evaluates true then the second one is returned, as if you had used the first one in a compound match expression. Boolean values can also be used as the first item in a pair, as it will be translated to a match that will always match ("*") or never match ("SALT_IFELSE_MATCH_NOTHING") a target system. This is essentially another way to express the ``filter_by`` functionality in way that's familiar to CFEngine or Oracle users. Consider using ``filter_by`` unless this function fits your workflow. CLI Example: salt '*' match.ifelse 'foo*' 'Foo!' 'bar*' 'Bar!' minion_id=bar03 match.ipcidr:

Append a rule to the specified table & chain. This function accepts a rule in a standard nftables command format, starting with the chain. Trying to force users to adapt to a new method of creating rules would be irritating at best, and we already have a parser that can handle it. CLI Example: salt '*' nftables.append filter input \ rule='tcp dport 22 log accept' IPv6: salt '*' nftables.append filter input \ rule='tcp dport 22 log accept' \ family=ipv6 nftables.build_rule:
Build a well-formatted nftables rule based on kwargs. A `table` and `chain` are not required, unless `full` is True. If `full` is `True`, then `table`, `chain` and `command` are required. `command` may be specified as either insert, append, or delete. This will return the nftables command, exactly as it would be used from the command line. If a position is required (as with `insert` or `delete`), it may be specified as `position`. This will only be useful if `full` is True. If `connstate` is passed in, it will automatically be changed to `state`. CLI Examples: salt '*' nftables.build_rule match=state \ connstate=RELATED,ESTABLISHED jump=ACCEPT salt '*' nftables.build_rule filter input command=insert position=3 \ full=True match=state state=related,established jump=accept IPv6: salt '*' nftables.build_rule match=state \ connstate=related,established jump=accept \ family=ipv6 salt '*' nftables.build_rule filter input command=insert position=3 \ full=True match=state state=related,established jump=accept \ family=ipv6 nftables.check:

This can be specified using the absolute path to the file, or using one of the following URL schemes: - ``salt://``, to fetch the file from the Salt fileserver. - ``http://`` or ``https://`` - ``ftp://`` - ``s3://`` - ``swift://`` commands The commands to send to the switch in config mode. Calls the master for a fresh pillar, generates the pillar data on the fly (same as :py:func:`items`) pillar If specified, allows for a dictionary of pillar data to be made available to pillar and ext_pillar rendering. these pillar variables will also override any variables of the same name in pillar or ext_pillar. pillar_enc If specified, the data passed in the ``pillar`` argument will be passed through this renderer to decrypt it. Note: This will decrypt on the minion side, so the specified renderer must be set up on the minion for this to work. Alternatively, pillar data can be decrypted master-side. For more information, see the :ref:`Pillar Encryption <pillar-encryption>` documentation. Pillar data that is decrypted master-side, is not decrypted until the end of pillar compilation though, so minion-side decryption will be necessary if the encrypted pillar data must be made available in an decrypted state pillar/ext_pillar rendering. pillarenv Pass a specific pillar environment from which to compile pillar data. If not specified, then the minion's :conf_minion:`pillarenv` option is not used, and if that also is not specified then all configured pillar environments will be merged into a single pillar dictionary and returned. saltenv Included only for compatibility with :conf_minion:`pillarenv_from_saltenv`, and is otherwise ignored. Changed in version 2016.3.6,2016.11.3,2017.7.0 The supported ext_pillar types are now tunable using the :conf_master:`on_demand_ext_pillar` config option. Earlier releases used a hard-coded default. Generate the pillar and apply an explicit external pillar external A single ext_pillar to add to the ext_pillar configuration. This must be passed as a single section from the ext_pillar configuration (see CLI examples below). For more complicated ``ext_pillar`` configurations, it can be helpful to use the Python shell to load YAML configuration into a dictionary, and figure out >>> import salt.utils.yaml >>> ext_pillar = salt.utils.yaml.safe_load(""" ... ext_pillar: ... - git: ... - issue38440 https://github.com/terminalmage/git_pillar: ... - env: base ... """) >>> ext_pillar {'ext_pillar': [{'git': [{'mybranch https://github.com/myuser/myrepo': [{'env': 'base'}]}]}]} >>> ext_pillar['ext_pillar'][0] {'git': [{'mybranch https://github.com/myuser/myrepo': [{'env': 'base'}]}]} In the above example, the value to pass would be ``{'git': [{'mybranch https://github.com/myuser/myrepo': [{'env': 'base'}]}]}``. Note that this would need to be quoted when passing on the CLI (as in the CLI examples below). pillar : None If specified, allows for a dictionary of pillar data to be made available to pillar and ext_pillar rendering. These pillar variables will also override any variables of the same name in pillar or ext_pillar. New in version 2015.5.0 CLI Examples: salt '*' pillar.ext '{libvirt: _}' salt '*' pillar.ext "{'git': ['master https://github.com/myuser/myrepo']}" salt '*' pillar.ext "{'git': [{'mybranch https://github.com/myuser/myrepo': [{'env': 'base'}]}]}" pillar.fetch:
New in version 0.14.0 Attempt to retrieve the named value from :ref:`in-memory pillar data <pillar-in-memory>`. If the pillar key is not present in the in-memory pillar, then the value specified in the ``default`` option (described below) will be returned. If the merge parameter is set to ``True``, the default will be recursively merged into the returned pillar data. The value can also represent a value in a nested dict using a ":" delimiter for the dict. This means that if a dict in pillar looks like this:: {'pkg': {'apache': 'httpd'}} To retrieve the value associated with the ``apache`` key in the ``pkg`` dict this key can be passed as:: pkg:apache key The pillar key to get value from default The value specified by this option will be returned if the desired pillar key does not exist. If a default value is not specified, then it will be an empty string, unless :conf_minion:`pillar_raise_on_missing` is set to ``True``, in which case an error will be raised. merge : ``False`` If ``True``, the retrieved values will be merged into the passed default. When the default and the retrieved value are both dictionaries, the dictionaries will be recursively merged. New in version 2014.7.0 Changed in version 2016.3.7,2016.11.4,2017.7.0 If the default and the retrieved value are not of the same type, then merging will be skipped and the retrieved value will be returned. Publish a command from the minion out to other minions. Publications need to be enabled on the Salt master and the minion needs to have permission to publish the command. The Salt master will also prevent a recursive publication loop, this means that a minion cannot command another minion to command another minion as that would create an infinite command loop. The ``tgt_type`` argument is used to pass a target other than a glob into the execution, the available options are: - glob - pcre - grain - grain_pcre - pillar - pillar_pcre - ipcidr - range - compound Changed in version 2017.7.0 The ``expr_form`` argument has been renamed to ``tgt_type``, earlier releases must use ``expr_form``. Note that for pillar matches must be exact, both in the pillar matcher and the compound matcher. No globbing is supported. The arguments sent to the minion publish function are separated with commas. Notes on:

  • Fashion: Developing a personal style, curating a wardrobe, and exploring fashion trends.
  • Grooming: Hair care, skincare, makeup, and personal hygiene routines.
  • Self-presentation: Body language, posture, and non-verbal communication.
  • Personal branding: Creating a consistent and authentic personal brand across online and offline platforms.

Quantified Self

  • Outfits worn per week
  • Items purchased (clothing, accessories, grooming products)
  • Money spent on fashion and grooming
  • Skincare routine consistency (days followed)
  • Haircare products used
  • Gym clothes vs. casual clothes ratio
  • Outfit changes per day
  • Laundry cycles completed
  • Dry cleaning visits
  • Tailoring or alterations done
  • Perfume/cologne bottles owned
  • Shoes owned vs. shoes worn
  • Capsules or coordinated outfits created
  • Seasonal wardrobe updates completed
  • Thrifted or second-hand items purchased
  • Impulse fashion purchases tracked
  • Clothing returns made
  • Donation boxes filled

Fashion

Developing a Personal Style

  • Identifying colour palettes that suit your skin tone
  • Understanding body types and what flatters them
  • Building a capsule wardrobe
  • Mixing high and low street pieces
  • Learning when to follow trends and when to ignore them

Wardrobe Essentials

The Basics

  • Well-fitting white t-shirts
  • Dark denim jeans
  • Black or navy chinos
  • A fitted blazer
  • A quality leather jacket
  • White sneakers
  • Black boots
  • A neutral knit sweater

Seasonal Additions

  • Lightweight coat for spring
  • Waterproof jacket for rain
  • Wool overcoat for winter
  • Linen shirts for summer

Shopping Smart

  • Buying less, buying better
  • Knowing your measurements before shopping online
  • Checking fabric composition (natural fibres tend to last longer)
  • Looking for sales and end-of-season clearances
  • Investing in tailoring — a £20 alteration can transform a £50 garment

Caring for Your Clothes

  • Washing less frequently (jeans, knitwear)
  • Using garment bags for storage
  • Learning basic sewing — button replacement, hemming
  • Proper shoe care (polishing, waterproofing)
  • Rotating shoes to extend their life

Grooming

Skincare

The Basics

  • Cleanser — morning and night
  • Moisturiser — suited to your skin type
  • Sunscreen — every day, even when it’s cloudy
  • Exfoliator — once or twice a week

Going Further

  • Serums (vitamin C, retinol, hyaluronic acid)
  • Eye cream
  • Face mask (clay, hydrating, exfoliating)
  • Lip balm
  • Hand cream

Skin Types and What Works

  • Oily skin: gel-based cleansers, oil-free moisturisers
  • Dry skin: cream cleansers, richer moisturisers, facial oils
  • Combination skin: balancing products, targeted treatment
  • Sensitive skin: fragrance-free, minimal ingredient lists

Haircare

  • Finding a barber or stylist you trust
  • Understanding your hair type (straight, wavy, curly, coily)
  • Washing frequency — most people wash too often
  • Conditioner is not optional
  • Scalp health matters — dry scalp means itchy scalp
  • Trimming regularly even if you’re growing it out
  • Product selection — pomade, clay, cream, sea salt spray

Personal Hygiene

  • Daily shower or bath
  • Deodorant — clinical strength if needed
  • Nail care — trimmed, clean, under control
  • Nose and ear hair trimming
  • Oral hygiene — flossing, tongue scraping, mouthwash
  • Foot care — exfoliation, moisturising, proper socks

Makeup (for Those Who Wear It)

  • Skincare first — makeup sits better on healthy skin
  • Less is more for everyday
  • Setting spray extends wear
  • Removing makeup properly before bed

Self-Presentation

Posture

  • Shoulders back, chin level
  • Standing with weight evenly distributed
  • Sitting without slouching — core engaged
  • The wall test: heels, calves, shoulders, head against a wall

Body Language

  • Eye contact — confident but not staring
  • Open gestures — avoid crossing arms defensively
  • Handshakes — firm, brief, dry
  • Mirroring — subtly matching the other person’s energy
  • Personal space — respecting boundaries

Voice and Speech

  • Speaking clearly and at a moderate pace
  • Avoiding vocal fry and uptalk
  • Pausing instead of filling silence with “um”
  • Matching your tone to the situation

Dressing for the Occasion

  • Knowing the dress code before you arrive
  • When in doubt, slightly overdressed beats underdressed
  • Fit matters more than brand
  • Clean, intact shoes go a long way

Personal Branding

Online Presence

  • LinkedIn — professional, updated, with a proper photo
  • Social media — what would you want a potential employer to find?
  • Consistent name and photo across platforms
  • A personal website or portfolio if relevant

Offline Presence

  • How you introduce yourself
  • Your email signature
  • Business cards (yes, still)
  • Consistency between what you say and how you present yourself

The Throughline

Your personal brand isn’t something you manufacture — it’s the consistent thread between who you are and how you show up. It emerges from repeated actions, not a single curated moment.

content:
I used to think self-promotion meant bragging. Turns out it just means making sure the right people know what you’ve done. There’s a difference, and learning it changed how I move through my career.
The people who get promoted aren’t always the best workers. They’re the ones whose work gets seen. That’s not a conspiracy — it’s just how organisations work. If nobody knows you shipped the thing that saved the quarter, you’re not going to get the promotion.
So here’s what I’ve picked up about getting credit for the work you actually do.
Own Your Words The easiest place to start is with language. When you talk about something you did, say “I” not “we”. Not because collaboration doesn’t matter — it does — but because “we” erases you. Your manager can’t advocate for someone they can’t identify.
This isn’t about taking credit for other people’s work. It’s about being precise. If you wrote the report, say you wrote the report. If you led the project, say you led it. You can acknowledge help without swallowing your contribution whole.
Make Your Manager Your Ally Your manager is the single most important relationship in your career at any given company. Not because they have power over you, but because they’re the one who talks about you when you’re not in the room.
Keep them informed. Send updates. Show them what you’ve done before they have to ask. A manager who knows your work can fight for you; a manager who doesn’t know your work can’t.
And if your manager isn’t doing this for you, that’s data. It tells you something about the relationship, and maybe about the organisation.
Use Performance Reviews Properly Yearly reviews are one of those institutional rituals everyone goes through, but most people treat them as a formality. Don’t. This is your moment to sit across from someone with authority and lay out exactly what you’ve delivered.
Prepare a document beforehand. List your achievements with dates, context, and impact. Not “I improved the process” but “I redesigned the onboarding workflow in March, which cut setup time from two weeks to three days.” Specificity is what separates a strong review from a forgettable one.
You’re not asking for permission to feel good about your work. You’re giving your manager the ammunition they need to make a case for you.
Be Visible Without Being Loud Speaking up in meetings matters, but there’s a difference between contributing and dominating. The goal isn’t to be the loudest voice — it’s to be the one people remember.
Ask thoughtful questions. Offer a perspective that shifts the conversation. Follow up after with an email summarising what you proposed, so there’s a paper trail and your name attached to the idea.
And make sure you’re engaging with the right people. Not just your immediate team, but the folks a few levels up who influence hiring and promotion decisions. A casual coffee chat or a well-timed question after a presentation can plant a seed.
Make Your Boss Look Good This sounds counterintuitive if you’re focused on yourself, but it’s one of the most effective strategies there is. When your manager succeeds, you succeed with them.
Share credit where it’s due, yes, but also share your results upward. If you delivered something significant, loop your manager in. Frame it as “we” when appropriate — the win is theirs too — but make sure your contribution is visible within that frame.
A manager who feels supported by you will advocate for you. A manager who feels threatened by you won’t. Read the room.
Build Alliances You don’t need to be everyone’s favourite, but you do need allies. People who’ve seen your work, trust your judgment, and are willing to mention your name in the right context.
Set up regular 1 on 1s with people across the organisation, not just your direct team. Learn what they’re working on. Offer help where you can. These relationships compound over time.
When the promotion conversation comes up, having three people who can vouch for you carries more weight than one manager doing all the talking.
Don’t Be the Person Who Makes Things Awkward None of this matters if you’re the colleague people resent. Don’t embarrass coworkers in public. Don’t steal credit for other people’s work — that reputation travels faster than anything else. Be competent, be reliable, and don’t make people regret supporting you.
Self-promotion has a ceiling. Cross it and you become someone nobody wants to work with, and no amount of visibility will save you.
Define What You’re Actually Trying to Get Before you invest energy in any of this, ask yourself what you want. A promotion? More interesting work? Higher pay? Different responsibilities?
The strategy changes depending on the answer. If you want to move up, visibility and alliances matter most. If you want better projects, making your manager look good and speaking up in the right forums will get you there. If you just want to do good work without the drama, sometimes the best promotion strategy is to be so reliable that people can’t ignore you.
Know your target. Everything else is just tactics.

content:
I’ve been thinking a lot about spirituality lately. Not in the abstract, philosophical sense — more like the practical, daily kind. The kind that shows up when you’re sitting in a room full of people and feel completely alone, or when you’re walking through a forest and suddenly remember to breathe.
This page is where I’m collecting my thoughts on the subject. It covers religion, philosophy, meditation, and everything in between. Some of it is personal, some of it is research, and some of it is just me trying to figure things out as I go.
Beliefs Religion Shia Islam I was raised Shia Muslim, specifically in the Ismaili tradition. It’s not something I think about every day, but it’s always there — like the background music in a film you can’t quite hear but know is playing.
Shia Imami Ismaili Muslim The Ismailis are a branch of Shia Islam that traces its leadership through the Imams, starting with Ali ibn Abi Talib and continuing in an unbroken line. For me, this isn’t just historical trivia. It’s a living connection — a sense that I’m part of something much bigger than myself, stretching back over a thousand years.
The current Imam, Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, is someone I look to for guidance. Not in a blind-following way, but more like how you might look to a mentor. He’s given me a framework for thinking about faith, service, and how to live in a modern world without losing your spiritual centre.
Ginans Ginans are devotional hymns that form part of the Ismaili spiritual tradition. They’re written in various languages — Sindhi, Hindi, Gujarati, Urdu — and they blend Islamic theology with local poetic forms. When I hear them sung, there’s something about the melody that gets under your skin.
They’re not just religious texts. They’re stories, prayers, and philosophy all wrapped into one. Some of my favourite ginans tell the stories of prophets, others explore the nature of the soul, and a few are just straight-up beautiful love poems — to God, obviously, but they read like anything but.
Quasidahs Quasidahs are another form of devotional poetry in the Ismaili tradition. They’re more structured than ginans — usually written in a specific meter and rhyme scheme. I find them less accessible than ginans, but there’s a discipline to them that I respect. They remind me that spirituality doesn’t have to be loose and free-form to be meaningful.
Nandi Nandi is a prayer of thanksgiving, usually said at the end of a gathering or ceremony. It’s a moment of collective gratitude — everyone in the room saying the same words at the same time. There’s something powerful about that synchronicity, even if you’re not deeply religious. It makes you feel like you’re part of a community, even if just for a few minutes.
Awal Sufro Awal Sufro is the first evening of Ramadan, when Ismailis gather for a special prayer and sermon. It’s one of those nights that marks the beginning of something. The atmosphere in the jamatkhana changes — there’s a sense of anticipation, like everyone is holding their breath together.
Festivals There are several festivals in the Ismaili calendar, each with its own significance:
Milad — The birthday of the Prophet Muhammad and his family. A time for reflection and celebration. Jashn-e-Berez — The spring equinox celebration, marking the new year in the Zoroastrian calendar. It’s one of those festivals that reminds me how many layers of tradition are woven into Ismaili practice. Eid-e-Milad-un-Nabi — Another celebration of the Prophet’s birthday, observed with special prayers and gatherings. Miraj Miraj refers to the Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad, when he is believed to have travelled from Mecca to Jerusalem and then ascended through the heavens. For Ismailis, this event has deeper esoteric meanings — it’s not just about the physical journey but about the soul’s ascent towards divine understanding.
I first learned about Miraj as a child, and it always struck me as one of those stories that sits somewhere between history and metaphor. Is it meant to be taken literally? Maybe. But even if it’s symbolic, the idea of a journey through different states of consciousness is pretty powerful.
Yawm e Ali Yawm e Ali, or the Day of Ali, commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm where the Prophet Muhammad is said to have designated Ali as his successor. It’s a significant day in Shia Islam and one that reinforces the importance of leadership and succession in our tradition.
For me, it’s less about the politics of succession and more about the idea of commitment — to a cause, to a community, to something larger than yourself.
Waez A waez is a sermon or religious discourse, usually given by a learned member of the community. I’ve attended many waezis over the years, and they vary enormously in quality. Some are genuinely moving — the kind that stay with you for days. Others feel like they’re going through the motions.
The best waezis are the ones that connect ancient texts to modern life. When a speaker can make you feel like a thousand-year-old verse is speaking directly to your current situation, that’s when religion feels alive.
Khidma Khidma means service, and it’s a core value in the Ismaili tradition. The Aga Khan has always emphasised the importance of serving your community and your country, regardless of your faith. It’s not just a nice idea — it’s practically woven into the fabric of Ismaili institutions.
I’ve done my fair share of khidma over the years, from volunteering at local events to helping with community projects. It’s not always glamorous, but it gives you a sense of purpose that other things rarely do.
Month of Rajab Rajab is the seventh month of the Islamic calendar and holds special significance for Ismailis. It’s a time of reflection, prayer, and preparation for the months ahead. The first evening of Rajab is marked with special gatherings and prayers.
I’ve noticed that during Rajab, there’s a different quality to the community — people seem more contemplative, more inclined to reach out to others. It’s a small thing, but it makes the month feel distinct from the rest of the year.
Shukravari Beej Shukravari Beej is the first Friday of Navroz (the Ismaili New Year). It’s celebrated with special prayers and gatherings, and it marks the beginning of the new year in the Farvardin calendar. The word “shukravari” comes from the Persian word for Friday, and “beej” means seed — so it’s something like the seeding of the new year.
I’ve always liked the imagery of it. There’s something hopeful about planting a seed and trusting that it will grow.
Laylat al-Qadr Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, is considered the holiest night in the Islamic calendar. It commemorates the night when the Quran was first revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. For Ismailis, it’s a time of intense prayer and reflection.
I remember spending many Laylat al-Qadr nights in the jamatkhana, sitting in the dark, listening to prayers being recited. There’s a particular kind of peace that comes from being in a room full of people who are all focused on the same thing at the same time.
Salgirah Salgirah is the celebration of an Imam’s birthday. It’s one of the most important events in the Ismaili calendar, and it’s marked with special prayers, gatherings, and feasts.
I used to wonder why we celebrate the Imam’s birthday when birthdays aren’t really a traditional Islamic practice. But then I thought about it differently: birthdays are a way of expressing love and gratitude for someone who matters to you. If the Imam is someone who matters deeply to the community, then celebrating his birth makes sense — not as a religious obligation, but as an expression of devotion.
Philosophy Stoicism Stoicism has been a useful framework for me, especially during difficult periods. The core idea is simple: some things are up to us, and some things aren’t. Focus on what you can control, accept what you can’t, and don’t waste energy worrying about the rest.
It’s not a particularly original insight, but it’s surprisingly hard to actually practice. I find myself returning to Stoic texts when life feels chaotic — usually Seneca or Marcus Aurelius.
Epictetus Epictetus was a former slave who became one of the most influential Stoic philosophers. His teachings, recorded by his student Arrian in the Discourses and the Enchiridion, are remarkably practical. He doesn’t deal in abstract metaphysics — he talks about how to live.
One of my favourite passages from the Enchiridion is the opening: “Some things are up to us, and some things are not up to us.” Everything that follows flows from that simple distinction.
Seneca Seneca was a statesman, playwright, and Stoic philosopher who lived in Rome during the first century AD. His letters to his friend Lucilius — collected as the Moral Letters to Lucilius — are some of the most readable philosophical writing ever produced.
What I appreciate about Seneca is his honesty about human weakness. He doesn’t pretend that wisdom is easy or that we’ll never slip up. He writes about frustration, anger, grief, and fear as if he’s experienced them himself — because he had.
Existentialism Existentialism appeals to me because it takes responsibility seriously. The existentialists — Sartre, de Beauvoir, Camus — argued that we are radically free and therefore radically responsible for our choices. There’s no predetermined essence, no cosmic plan, no excuse.
That can be terrifying, but it’s also liberating. If life has no inherent meaning, then I get to decide what meaning has. It’s a heavy burden, but it’s mine.
Jean-Paul Sartre Sartre is the existentialist most people have heard of, and for good reason. His idea that “existence precedes essence” — that we exist first and then define ourselves through our actions — is both simple and devastating.
I’ve always been struck by his honesty about the anxiety that comes with freedom. He didn’t pretend that being free was comfortable. It’s not. But he argued that it’s unavoidable, and that pretending otherwise is what he called “bad faith.”
Simone de Beauvoir De Beauvoir was a sharper thinker than Sartre, in my opinion. Her Second Sex is still one of the most important works of feminist philosophy, and her ethical writings — especially The Ethics of Ambiguity — offer a more nuanced take on existentialism than Sartre’s.
What I appreciate about de Beauvoir is her attention to the concrete details of lived experience. She doesn’t just talk about abstract freedom — she talks about what it feels like to be constrained by gender, by class, by circumstance.
Humanism Humanism, broadly speaking, is the view that human beings are capable of leading ethical and meaningful lives without reference to supernatural beliefs. It’s not anti-religious — many humanists are religious — but it does place the focus on human agency and human experience.
I find humanism appealing because it takes human suffering seriously without offering easy answers. It doesn’t promise that everything happens for a reason. It says: things are hard, but we can make them better, and that’s enough.
Renaissance Humanism Renaissance humanism was a cultural and intellectual movement that emphasised the study of classical texts, the importance of education, and the potential of human beings. It emerged in Italy in the fourteenth century and spread across Europe.
What strikes me about Renaissance humanists is their optimism about human potential. They believed that through education and self-improvement, people could achieve greatness. It’s a refreshing contrast to some of the more pessimistic philosophical traditions.
Secular Humanism Secular humanism is the modern offshoot of humanist thought. It explicitly rejects religious belief and instead grounds ethics in human reason and experience. Prominent secular humanists include Bertrand Russell, Carl Sagan, and Margaret Atwood.
I appreciate secular humanism’s commitment to evidence and reason, but I also think it can sometimes underestimate the role that ritual, community, and transcendence play in human life. Not everyone needs a God to find meaning, but not everyone is satisfied by reason alone either.
Meditation Transcendental Meditation (TM) TM is a specific form of mantra meditation that was popularised in the West by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. Practitioners sit comfortably with their eyes closed and silently repeat a mantra — a specific sound or phrase — for about twenty minutes, twice a day.
I’ve tried TM on and off over the years. It’s not particularly difficult, but it does require consistency. The benefit I’ve noticed is subtle: a general sense of calm that seems to linger after practice, rather than any dramatic spiritual experience.
Mantra Meditation Mantra meditation involves repeating a word, phrase, or sound — either aloud or silently — to focus the mind. It’s found in many traditions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, and even some Christian contemplative practices.
What I like about mantra meditation is its simplicity. You don’t need any special equipment or training — just a mantra and a few minutes of quiet. The challenge is keeping the mind from wandering, but that’s true of most meditation practices.
Yogic Flying Yogic Flying is a practice associated with the Divine Life Society and the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. Practitioners sit on the ground and gently bounce or float, supposedly generating cosmic energy.
I’ll be honest — I’m sceptical about Yogic Flying. It looks strange, and the claims made about it seem exaggerated. But I suppose if it works for people, who am I to judge? Meditation is personal, and what works for one person might not work for another.
Loving-kindness Meditation Loving-kindness meditation, or metta meditation, involves cultivating feelings of goodwill and compassion towards oneself and others. You typically start by directing loving-kindness towards yourself, then towards a loved one, then towards a neutral person, then towards a difficult person, and finally towards all beings.
I find this practice genuinely moving. It’s easier to feel compassion for a stranger than for someone you have a complicated relationship with, which is probably the point. The practice reveals how conditional our kindness often is.
Metta Bhavana Metta bhavana is the Pali term for loving-kindness meditation. It’s a central practice in Theravada Buddhism and has been adapted by many secular mindfulness programmes.
The practice involves systematically extending feelings of metta (loving-kindness) from yourself outwards to increasingly wider circles of beings. It’s a way of training the mind to be more compassionate, and research suggests it can actually change how people respond to others.
Tonglen Tonglen is a Tibetan Buddhist meditation practice that involves breathing in suffering and breathing out compassion. It’s a powerful practice, but it’s not for beginners — it can be emotionally intense.
The idea is that by willingly taking in the suffering of others (symbolically, through the breath), you develop compassion and reduce your own ego-centredness. It’s a counterintuitive practice, but one that many people find deeply transformative.
Zen Meditation Zen meditation, or zazen, is the practice of sitting in silence and observing the mind without attachment. There’s no mantra, no visualisation — just sitting, breathing, and watching thoughts arise and pass away.
I’ve tried zazen a few times, and I always come away feeling like I didn’t do it “right.” But that might be the point. Zen is less about achieving a particular state and more about seeing clearly what’s already there.
Zazen Zazen is the Japanese term for seated meditation in the Zen tradition. Practitioners sit in a specific posture — usually cross-legged on a cushion, with hands resting in the lap and eyes half-closed. The focus is on posture and breath, not on any particular technique.
What I appreciate about zazen is its simplicity. There’s nothing to achieve, nothing to attain. You just sit. The difficulty is in the sitting — in letting go of the constant urge to do something, to fix something, to become something.
Koan Practice A koan is a riddle or paradox used in Zen meditation to provoke doubt and transcend logical thinking. The most famous koan is “What is the sound of one hand clapping?” — but there are thousands of others.
Koan practice is meant to short-circuit the analytical mind and lead to direct insight. I’ve never been able to “solve” a koan, but I’ve found that sitting with one for a while can be surprisingly relaxing. It forces you to stop thinking so hard about everything.
Connection Nature I’ve always felt a particular kind of peace in nature. It’s not just the scenery — though that helps — but the sense of scale. When you’re standing in a forest or on a mountaintop, your problems feel smaller, not because they’ve changed but because everything else has expanded.
Outdoor Retreats I’ve done a few outdoor retreats over the years — some spiritual, some secular. The common thread is that they remove you from your normal environment and force you to pay attention to something other than your daily routine.
The best retreats are the ones that don’t try too hard. You don’t need elaborate programmes or charismatic leaders. Sometimes all you need is a quiet place, some company, and time to think.
Forest Bathing Forest bathing, or shinrin-yoku, is a Japanese practice of spending time in the forest for health and well-being. It’s not about exercise or hiking — it’s about being present in the forest, engaging all your senses.
I tried it once on a walk through a woodland near my house, and I was surprised by how different it felt from a normal walk. When you slow down and actually pay attention — to the smell of the leaves, the sound of the wind, the quality of the light — the forest becomes a different place.
Wilderness Survival I’ve never taken a wilderness survival course, but I’ve always been drawn to the idea. There’s something appealing about being able to provide for yourself in a natural environment — to find shelter, start a fire, purify water.
It’s not just about practical skills, though. I think wilderness survival also teaches you something about your own capacity to cope with difficulty. When you’re stripped of your modern conveniences, you discover what you’re actually made of.
Eco-tourism Eco-tourism is travel that minimises environmental impact and supports local communities. I’ve done a bit of eco-tourism over the years — staying in lodges, visiting national parks, volunteering on conservation projects.
What I’ve learned is that travel doesn’t have to be destructive. You can see the world without leaving a trail of carbon and waste, if you’re willing to slow down and pay attention.
Sustainable Travel Sustainable travel is about making choices that reduce your environmental impact while travelling. It can be as simple as taking a train instead of a plane, or as complex as offsetting your carbon footprint through verified programmes.
I’m not perfect at this — I still fly more than I should — but I’ve been trying to be more conscious about it. Every trip is a chance to make better choices, even if they’re small.
Wildlife Conservation Wildlife conservation is important to me, both as a practical concern and as a moral one. The rate at which species are going extinct is alarming, and it’s largely driven by human activity.
I’ve supported various conservation organisations over the years, and I try to be informed about the issues. It’s easy to feel powerless in the face of something as large-scale as biodiversity loss, but individual actions add up — and collective action starts with individual awareness.
Nature Walks Nature walks are my go-to form of exercise and meditation. I don’t need a trail or a summit — a patch of green is enough. There’s something about walking in nature that clears my head in a way that walking in a city never does.
I’ve noticed that the best walks are the unplanned ones. The ones where you just put on your shoes and go, without a route or a destination in mind.
Birdwatching Tours I’ve never been a serious birdwatcher, but I’ve done a few tours over the years and found them surprisingly enjoyable. There’s something calming about trying to identify birds by their song or silhouette — it forces you to slow down and pay attention.
If I were to get more into birdwatching, I’d probably start with a good field guide and spend time in my local park. You’d be surprised how many species you can find if you just look.
Photography Walks Photography walks combine walking with photography, usually in a natural or urban setting. I’ve done a few of these, both as part of organised groups and on my own.
What I’ve learned is that photography changes the way you see. When you’re looking for a good shot, you notice things you would otherwise miss — the way light falls on a wall, the pattern of leaves on the ground, the expression on a stranger’s face.
Community Religious Communities Religious communities have been important to me throughout my life. The jamatkhana — the Ismaili place of worship — has been a constant source of support, friendship, and belonging.
What I’ve learned from religious communities is that belief alone isn’t enough. You need a community to practice your beliefs with, to challenge you, to support you, and to celebrate with you. Faith is not a solo endeavour.
Monastic Communities I’ve never lived in a monastic community, but I’ve visited a few and spent time with monks and nuns from various traditions. What strikes me about monastic life is the intentionality — every aspect of daily life is designed to support spiritual growth.
It’s not a lifestyle I could sustain, but I admire the commitment. There’s something admirable about choosing to simplify your life in service of something larger than yourself.
Spiritual Retreats Spiritual retreats have been a recurring feature of my life. Some have been religious — pilgrimages, prayer gatherings, fasting periods. Others have been secular — mindfulness retreats, meditation intensives, yoga holidays.
The common thread is that they all remove you from your normal routine and give you space to think, breathe, and be. I’ve found that even a weekend retreat can shift your perspective in ways that weeks of ordinary life don’t.
Social Groups Social groups — whether formal or informal — are essential for well-being. Research consistently shows that strong social connections are one of the best predictors of happiness and longevity.
I’ve learned this the hard way. There have been periods in my life when I was socially isolated, and I can tell you that it takes a toll — on your mental health, your physical health, and your sense of purpose.
Interest-based Clubs Interest-based clubs are a great way to meet people who share your passions. I’ve been part of book clubs, hiking groups, photography societies, and more. What I’ve found is that shared interests are a surprisingly effective icebreaker.
You don’t need to have deep conversations with someone to enjoy their company. Sometimes you just need to agree on something — a book, a trail, a film — and build from there.
Volunteer Organizations Volunteering has been a significant part of my life, both through Ismaili institutions and through secular organisations. It’s one of those things that sounds simple but has a profound impact — on the people you help and on yourself.
I’ve learned that volunteering is not about saviourism. It’s about solidarity — recognising that we’re all in this together and doing what we can to make things better.
Support Groups Support groups have been invaluable for me at various points in my life. Whether it’s a grief support group, a mental health group, or a recovery group, the shared experience of struggle creates a bond that’s hard to find elsewhere.
What I’ve learned from support groups is that vulnerability is not weakness. Sharing your struggles with others doesn’t make you a burden — it makes you human, and it often helps others who are going through similar things.
Recovery Groups Recovery groups — whether for addiction, grief, or other life challenges — are built on the idea that sharing your story can be healing. The twelve-step tradition, in particular, emphasises the importance of sponsorship, community, and service.
I’ve attended a few recovery meetings over the years, and what strikes me is how honest people are. There’s no pretence, no performance — just people telling the truth about their lives. That honesty is rare and precious.
Grief Support Groups Grief support groups are for people who have lost someone close to them. They’re not always easy to attend — grief is raw and uncomfortable — but they can be incredibly helpful.
What I’ve learned from grief support groups is that grief doesn’t follow a timeline. There’s no right way to grieve, and there’s no point at which you’re “done.” You learn to carry your loss with you, and over time, it becomes part of who you are.
Inner Self Self-reflection Self-reflection is the practice of examining your thoughts, feelings, and behaviours. It’s something I’ve tried to do regularly, though not always successfully.
I find that journaling is one of the most effective forms of self-reflection. Writing down your thoughts forces you to slow down and organise them, and it often reveals patterns you wouldn’t notice otherwise.
Meditation Retreats Meditation retreats are intensive periods of practice, usually lasting from a few days to several weeks. They’re challenging — sitting in silence for extended periods can bring up difficult emotions — but they’re also transformative.
I’ve done a few meditation retreats, and each one has taught me something different. The common thread is that silence is not empty. When you stop filling every moment with noise, you start to hear what’s been there all along.
Solo Travel Solo travel has been one of the most valuable experiences of my life. There’s something about being alone in an unfamiliar place that forces you to confront yourself. You can’t hide from your thoughts when there’s no one else around.
I’ve travelled solo through Europe, Asia, and Africa, and each trip has taught me something about who I am and what I want. The lessons are rarely what you expect — they’re usually about your own reactions, not the places you visit.
Spiritual Retreats I’ve already mentioned spiritual retreats, but they deserve a second mention because they’re so important. Whether religious or secular, retreats give you the space to step outside your normal life and pay attention to what matters.
I’ve found that the best retreats are the ones that don’t programme every minute. Some of my most valuable moments have been in the unstructured time — walking alone, sitting in silence, writing in a journal.
Silent Retreats Silent retreats are exactly what they sound like — periods of silence, usually lasting from a day to several weeks. You don’t speak, you don’t use your phone, you don’t read or write. You just sit, walk, and eat in silence.
I did a three-day silent retreat once, and it was one of the hardest and most rewarding things I’ve ever done. By the second day, my mind was racing — full of thoughts, memories, anxieties. By the third day, it had settled into something quieter. I didn’t have any profound revelations, but I did have a sense of peace that lasted for weeks afterwards.
Vision Quests Vision quests are a Native American practice involving a period of solitude in nature, often accompanied by fasting, to seek spiritual guidance. I’ve never done a vision quest, but I understand the appeal — there’s something primal about spending time alone in the wilderness and asking the big questions.
I think many people do informal vision quests without realising it — periods of solitude, reflection, and connection with nature. You don’t need a cultural framework to benefit from sitting alone in the woods and thinking about your life.
Mindfulness Practices Mindfulness is the practice of paying attention to the present moment without judgment. It’s been popularised in recent years, but it has roots in many spiritual traditions.
I’ve found mindfulness useful for managing anxiety and staying present. It’s not a cure-all, but it’s a tool — like any tool, it works better with practice.
Walking Meditation Walking meditation is the practice of bringing mindfulness to the act of walking. You pay attention to each step, to the sensation of your feet touching the ground, to the movement of your body.
It’s simpler than it sounds, but harder than it looks. I’ve found that walking meditation is particularly useful when sitting meditation feels impossible — when my mind is too restless to be still.
Eating Meditation Eating meditation involves bringing full attention to the act of eating. You notice the colours, textures, flavours, and smells of your food. You eat slowly, without distraction.
It sounds trivial, but it’s surprisingly difficult to eat without scrolling through your phone or watching TV. When you actually pay attention to your food, it becomes a more satisfying experience — and you tend to eat less because you’re actually aware of when you’re full.
Body Scan Meditation Body scan meditation involves systematically bringing attention to different parts of your body, usually starting at your toes and working your way up to your head. It’s a form of mindfulness that helps you notice tension, discomfort, or relaxation in different parts of your body.
I’ve found body scan meditation useful for sleep — it helps me relax and let go of the day’s tensions. It’s also a good way to check in with yourself, to see where you’re holding stress or emotion.
Practices Prayer Prayer is a practice I’ve maintained throughout my life, though the form it takes has changed. As a child, prayer was something I did because I was told to. As an adult, it’s something I do because I want to — a way of connecting with something larger than myself.
I’ve found that prayer doesn’t have to be formal or structured. Sometimes it’s a ritualised recitation, sometimes it’s silent contemplation, and sometimes it’s just sitting quietly and thinking about what matters to you.
Daily Prayers Daily prayers are a central practice in Islam, with five prescribed prayer times throughout the day. For Ismailis, the form and timing may vary, but the principle remains — prayer as a regular practice of remembrance and connection.
I’ve tried to maintain a daily prayer practice for most of my adult life, though there have been gaps. What I’ve learned is that consistency matters more than perfection. It’s better to pray a little every day than to pray a lot once in a while.
Morning Prayers Morning prayers set the tone for the day. I’ve found that starting the day with a few minutes of prayer or meditation helps me feel grounded and focused.
There’s something about the quiet of the morning — before the world gets loud — that makes it a good time for reflection. Even if you only have five minutes, it’s enough to centre yourself before the day begins.
Evening Prayers Evening prayers are a way of closing the day — of reflecting on what happened, expressing gratitude, and letting go of what you can’t control.
I’ve found evening prayers particularly useful during difficult periods. They give me a chance to process what I’ve been through and prepare for the next day.
Rituals Rituals are structured practices that mark important moments in our lives. They can be religious — like baptism, confirmation, or marriage — or secular — like birthdays, anniversaries, or graduations.
What I’ve learned from rituals is that they matter. They give us a way of marking time, of creating meaning, of connecting with something larger than ourselves. Even if you don’t believe in the supernatural aspects of a ritual, the psychological benefits are real.
Religious Ceremonies Religious ceremonies — whether weddings, funerals, or festivals — are important social and spiritual events. They bring people together, mark transitions, and reinforce shared values.
I’ve attended many religious ceremonies over the years, and I’ve noticed that the ones that resonate most are the ones that feel authentic. You can tell when a ceremony is being performed out of habit versus when it’s being performed with genuine feeling.
Baptism Baptism is a Christian ritual of purification and initiation, usually involving water. It’s not part of my own tradition, but I’ve attended many baptisms and have always been struck by the significance people attach to them.
There’s something universal about the idea of washing away the old and starting fresh. It’s a powerful metaphor, regardless of your religious beliefs.
Confirmation Confirmation is a Christian rite of passage, usually occurring in adolescence, in which a person affirms the faith commitments made on their behalf at baptism. It’s a moment of personal commitment — a way of saying “this is my choice, not just my parents’.”
I appreciate the idea behind confirmation, even though I don’t practice it. The notion that faith should be a personal choice, not just an inherited tradition, is one I agree with.
Celebrations Celebrations — whether religious, cultural, or personal — are important for well-being. They give us a reason to pause, to connect with others, and to mark the passage of time.
I’ve learned that celebrations don’t need to be grand or expensive. A dinner with friends, a walk in the park, a quiet evening at home — these can be just as meaningful as a big event.
Festivals Festivals are communal celebrations that mark important dates in the religious or cultural calendar. They bring people together, reinforce shared identity, and provide a break from ordinary routine.
I’ve celebrated many festivals over the years — Eid, Navroz, Christmas, Diwali — and I’ve always appreciated the sense of continuity they provide. Festivals connect us to our past and to each other.
Rites of Passage Rites of passage mark important transitions in life — birth, coming of age, marriage, death. They’re found in every culture and religion, and they serve an important function: they help us navigate change.
What I’ve learned from rites of passage is that transitions are harder when they’re unmarked. Having a ritual to mark a change — even a small one — gives it weight and meaning.
Mindfulness Daily Mindfulness Practices Daily mindfulness practices can be simple — a few minutes of breathing, a moment of gratitude, a walk without your phone. The key is consistency, not duration.
I’ve found that even small mindfulness practices can have a significant impact on my day-to-day life. They don’t eliminate stress or problems, but they help me respond to them more skillfully.
Mindful Breathing Mindful breathing is the practice of paying attention to your breath. It’s the simplest form of meditation and one of the most effective.
When I’m feeling anxious or overwhelmed, I often return to mindful breathing. It’s a way of anchoring myself in the present moment, of reminding my body that I’m safe.
Mindful Eating I’ve already mentioned mindful eating, but it deserves emphasis because it’s one of the easiest ways to practice mindfulness. Every meal is an opportunity to be present — to taste your food, to notice your hunger and fullness, to appreciate the effort that went into preparing your meal.
Mindful Movement Mindful movement includes practices like yoga, tai chi, and qigong — activities that combine physical movement with mental attention. They’re a good way to bring mindfulness into your body, not just your mind.
I’ve found mindful movement particularly useful for managing stress and improving focus. It’s also a reminder that mindfulness isn’t just about sitting still — it can be practiced in motion.
Tai Chi Tai chi is a Chinese martial art that’s practised as a form of moving meditation. It involves slow, deliberate movements combined with deep breathing and mental focus.
I’ve tried tai chi a few times and found it relaxing, though I’m not skilled enough to do it properly. The idea — that movement can be a form of meditation — is one I find compelling.
Qigong Qigong is similar to tai chi but focuses more on breath and energy work. It’s a Chinese practice that combines movement, breathing, and meditation to cultivate qi (life energy).
I’ve found qigong to be a gentle form of exercise that also has a meditative quality. It’s not as physically demanding as other forms of exercise, but it leaves me feeling calm and centred.
Yoga Asanas Yoga asanas are the physical postures practised in yoga. They’re often the most visible aspect of yoga in the West, but they’re just one part of a much larger practice.
I’ve done yoga on and off for many years, and I’ve found it useful for both physical and mental well-being. The postures improve flexibility and strength, and the emphasis on breath and awareness has a calming effect.
This page will grow as my thinking evolves. For now, it’s a starting point — a collection of notes, questions, and reflections on spirituality in all its forms. If you’re interested in any of these topics, I’d love to hear your thoughts.
summary:
I’ve been thinking a lot about spirituality lately. Not in the abstract, philosophical sense — more like the practical, daily kind. The kind that shows up when you’re sitting in a room full of people and feel completely alone, or when you’re walking through a forest and suddenly remember to breathe.

This page is where I’m collecting my thoughts on the subject. It covers religion, philosophy, meditation, and everything in between. Some of it is personal, some of it is research, and some of it is just me trying to figure things out as I go.

Chapter 1.0 - What is an Amazing Life? As we embark on our journey of self-discovery and personal growth, one of the fundamental questions we must confront is: What is an amazing life? This question, simple as it may seem, has profound implications. The answer is not only a reflection of our beliefs, values, and priorities, but it also influences our actions and decisions. It is the lighthouse that guides us when we are lost at sea, the North Star that helps us navigate our way through the complexities of existence.
In this chapter, we will explore the concept of an amazing life from various perspectives, delving into scientific research, psychological theories, and philosophical considerations. Section 1: Psychological Perspectives on an Amazing Life
Psychology offers valuable insights about the key components that make life amazing, embracing various theories and paradigms.

It is essential to water these seeds within us—pursue activities that evoke positive emotions, engage in tasks that are challenging and meaningful, foster good relationships, and celebrate our achievements.
One significant psychological principle is Abraham Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.
Maslow posited that human needs are hierarchical—with physiological needs at the base, followed by safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.
To cultivate an amazing life, we must attend to these needs. It is essential to ensure our basic needs are met—for once they are met, we could focus on satisfying our psychological needs, paving the way to reach the pinnacle of self-actualization—living a life that is genuinely ‘us’.
Section 2: Philosophical Perspectives
Philosophy, the love of wisdom, has since time immemorial teased out the nuances of what might constitute an amazing life.
Paramount to philosophy is the pursuit of ‘Good Life’—summarised by the splendid Greek term, Eudaimonia. It translates to a ’life well-lived’—one marked by virtue and excellence.
Philosophy underscores the importance of virtues like courage, temperance, justice, and wisdom. The cultivation and manifestation of these virtues in daily life elevate our existence to that of Eudaimonia.
And it’s not just Hercules who should aspire for these virtues—all individuals, regardless of their station in life, can seek to instantiate these virtues.
Section 3: Scientific Considerations
Modern scientific research into wellbeing, satisfaction, and happiness provides yet another vantage point to understand an amazing life. The new science of positive psychology specifically focuses on human strengths and virtues, and how to foster them.
Noted positive psychologist Martin Seligman developed a robust model of wellbeing known as PERMA – standing for Positive Emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Achievement.
According to Seligman, the presence of these elements infuses life with a sense of fulfilment, happiness, and purpose, contributing to what can be considered an amazing life.

Chapter 1.1 - Defining what an amazing life should mean Before we delve into this captivating chapter, let’s first explore the core concept of an ‘amazing life.’ What does it mean to you? While some of us might envision a life filled to the brim with thrill and adrenaline, others could dream of a quiet life of contemplation and serenity. Remember, the beauty of life lies in its diversity, which allows each of us to have our individual interpretations of ‘amazing.’
In harmony with this thought, our aim in this chapter is not to impose a singular definition. Instead, we will pick apart the elements that generally contribute to creating an amazing life - one that’s brimming with happiness, purpose, satisfaction, and personal growth. The perspectives brought forth will be seasoned with insights from scientific research, renowned books, and reputable studies.
Elements of an ‘Amazing Life’ Before embarking on the journey of achieving an amazing life, it is essential to understand its basic composition. Here are a few key ingredients:
Happiness and Fulfillment
Happiness is often used as a barometer for a good life. However, equating momentary joy to having an amazing life can be misleading. A deep sense of fulfillment that stems from personal growth, meaningful relationships, and contentment, is, therefore, a more apt measure. Make a mental note of this subtle, yet significant difference.
Physical and Mental Health
Good health, comprised of both physical and mental well-being, is one of the most crucial pillars of an amazing life. It becomes vital, then, to commit to nourishing our bodies and minds.
Achieving Personal Goals
An amazing life is one where personal goals, whether related to career, relationships, financial stability, or personal development, are continuously chased and achieved. The sense of accomplishment derived from this pursuit adds layers of purpose and motivation.
Balance
A prominent characteristic of an amazing life is balance. Balance between work and play, giving and receiving, solitude, and social presence enables us to lead a meaningful and wholesome life.
Having explored these elements, we should acknowledge that an amazing life isn’t perfect. It’s perfectly normal to experience periods of trial and tribulation, but they pave the way for a richer life experience. As we embrace the concept of an ‘amazing life’ let’s envision it as a unique tapestry of experiences, emotions, and growth-endeavors that shape a life worth cherishing.

To explain the above diagram, let’s take it step by step. The image is a circle divided into four pieces of equal sizes - each quadrant represents a vital ingredient to lead an amazing life. Starting from the top right quadrant and moving clockwise, we begin with ‘Happiness and Fulfillment,’ which emphasizes the importance of cherishing happiness in every moment, and drawing fulfillment from our accomplishments. Goals can vary from person to person, but having something to aim for is essential for personal growth. Every piece of the quadrant touches the centre, indicating that each factor contributes equally to painting the larger picture of an ‘amazing life.’
Now, having defined what constitutes an amazing life, we must strive to comprehend how we can mold our current life trajectory to this ideal.
1. Your Amazing Life: Turning the Ideal into Reality
Life is a constantly evolving journey rather than a destination. The pursuit of an amazing life, similarly, is not a one-off sprint but a life-long marathon. We must embed the elements of an amazing life in our daily routine and make consistent efforts to nourish them.
Throughout this segment, we will explore actionable steps to facilitate this transformation. Here, too, we must remember that the suggestions put forth are not etched in stone. Feel free to adapt them to your unique circumstance and needs.
2. Designing Your Happiness
Happiness varies widely among individuals. To ensure a constant supply of joy and fulfillment, identify activities that genuinely make you happy.
Exercise: Identify Your Happy Triggers
Start by taking some time off your day to reflect on moments or activities where you’ve felt pure joy and fulfillment. List down these ‘happy triggers.’ They can range from simple pleasures like reading a book or enjoying a coffee, to grand experiences like travelling or playing a musical instrument.
Aim to incorporate at least one happy trigger into your routine every day. By consciously prioritizing moments of happiness and fulfillment, you’re taking control of your emotional landscape and sewing seeds for an amazing life.
3. Cultivating Health
In our pursuit of happiness and success, we often overlook our health. However, neglecting health can thwart our efforts in the long run.
Exercise: Building A Healthy Routine
Create a routine that respects your physical and mental health. Start with easy-to-achieve health goals like taking a walk every day, meditating for 10 minutes, or introducing more fruits and vegetables into your diet.
Remember, the focus is on consistent effort rather than radical changes. As you become comfortable with these initiatives, gradually set more challenging goals.
4. Chase Your Goals
In addition to enhancing our skills and knowledge, setting and achieving personal goals can give us a sense of purpose and drive.
Exercise: Goal Setting
Start by identifying areas of your life where you’d like to see growth or improvement. They could be related to your career, finances, health, relationships, or personal growth. For each area, set a ‘SMART’ goal - Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Use specific strategies and action plans to attain these goals.
5. Strike a Balance
To lead an amazing life, it is vital to maintain a balance in all the various facets of our life.
Exercise: Balancing Act
Conduct a self-assessment to identify areas of your life where you might be over or under-investing your time and energy. Devise an action plan to restore the balance.
As we wrap up this chapter, make a pact with yourself to incorporate these actions into your daily life. Remember, the journey to an amazing life is a marathon, not a sprint. Take it one step at a time.
Play of the Day
Before you retire, reflect on your day. Identify at least one activity that inched you closer to an amazing life. How did it make you feel? Document this detail in your journal. Use these reflections to steer your journey to an amazing life.
